```text
Peak Poker Performance

      (the majority of my play), boredom is less of a factor than live
      but the bigger danger is auto-piloting. I have a short sequence
      of questions to consider for dealing with certain situations, but
      in the moment I frequently find myself not applying these
      questions. This may be related to my second question which is,
          2. Are there any good techniques to use to slow down in
      game before making a decision? I have in mind online MTTs
      where the poker site limits the amount of time available and I
      am often multi-tabling. I find that I get into a rhythm of mak-
      ing hasty decisions even though I have more time left.
                                                                          Steve

    As I read over these two questions, a few thoughts came to mind.
First, it is important to take regular breaks. Most people know about 24-
hour circadian rhythms, which dictate wake and sleep cycles, but are un-
aware that our bodies operate another set of cycles called ultradian
rhythms, which last for 90–120 minutes. Functionally, this means that
our minds operate best when we take a break every 90–120 minutes. If
you play longer than this, you may notice the quality of your focus and
attention declines rapidly. Taking a 5–10 minute break is usually sufficient
to get you back on track. In this time, you want to get up and stretch a
bit. Take a couple of deep breaths and maybe grab a drink of water. Make
sure you step away from all things digital during this break to give your
mind a few minutes to recover.
    One of the best long-term methods for increasing focus and attention is
to start a regular meditation practice. Even just doing a few minutes each
day improves focus. The key is to make it a regular and consistent habit.
    Also, make sure that you do not have any distractions. Don’t look at
your phone, watch movies at the table or spend time on twitter. The brain
is not able to multi-task, contrary to what many believe. Every time you
switch your attention to a new task, your brain has to shift the way its
resources are allocated and that is not an efficient process. Do yourself a
favor by focusing as much as you can on playing poker and nothing else.
```

```text
                                                        Readers’ Questions

    I love the fact that you have a set of questions that you go through for
interesting or difficult spots. That’s a great way to alleviate boredom and
give yourself a clear focus during hands. Make sure that you keep them
where you can see them and refer to them often. This could help you
slow down. Making hasty decisions is a symptom of the brain working on
autopilot, which is actually its preferred method. The brain has two sys-
tems – the reflexive and the reflective. The reflexive system acts fairly
automatically and takes the path of least resistance. We usually defer to
this system when we are tired, tilted, or distracted. This is another reason
to make sure you are well rested and take plenty of breaks. The reflective
system is the part of the brain that engages in effortful decision making.
It takes more energy to operate the reflective system, but it is worth
making the effort!

August 14.
```

```text
                                                        Mastering Tilt



    Two Minute Meditation
It is a little known fact that allowing your eyes to rest in a soft
downward gaze has a fairly quick relaxing effect on the body. Here
are the steps to take:


   1. Sit up straight in a comfortable position.
   2. Allow your eyes to rest comfortably in a downward position.
      Maintain a soft gaze that is not focused on anything in par-
      ticular.
   3. Without completely closing your eyes, let your eyelids drop
      just a bit to a level that is comfortable.
   4. Continue your soft downward gaze and you will quickly start
      to feel relaxed. If your eyes become heavy, it is okay to let
      them close. Continue this for a minute or two until you are
      ready to get back into the game.



    Reality Therapy
Reality therapy, developed by Dr. William Glasser (2011), is based on
choice theory. It is also a form of cognitive behavioral treatment and
many people have found good results with it. Like Ellis, Glasser was
dissatisfied with the lack of results that his clients got from insight
oriented therapies and he theorized and experimented until he
found a system that worked.
The basis of choice theory is that all human beings are motivated by
four basic needs: belonging or love, power, fun, and freedom. The
need to belong and be involved with other people drives all human
```

```text
Positive Poker

beings, according to Glasser. There are multiple types of belonging
because we are all part of multiple groups (social, work, family, etc.).
The need for power is also the need for achievement, self-worth, and
recognition, and involves a certain level of competitiveness. Setting
goals and following through on them can also fulfill as a sense of
power. Glasser included fun as one of the four basic human needs
because he believed that most learning occurs when we are having
fun. Making work fun is important, too. Freedom is the last need
that Glasser considered. Humans have an innate need to make their
own choices and to be internally free. Choosing how you will re-
spond to bad events is a type of internal freedom. While we may
vary in our level of need, we all share a common bond of having
these four needs and we will spend vast amounts of time trying to
meet them.
Glasser argues that we use thinking, doing, feelings, and physiology
to help get us what we want. Perhaps we have the idea that winning
a poker championship will bring us money (power and freedom) and
fans (belonging), and be plenty fun. We will be very motivated to
win that championship because we believe it is going to meet just
about all our inherent needs. What if we start losing? Glasser said
that when our basic drives are blocked, we naturally feel frustrated
and this can cause us to make poor choices like going on tilt. When
we feel frustrated we become motivated to execute some behavior
which we believe will negate our frustration. Glasser would say that
you choose to go on tilt because it’s the best way you know to react
in the moment. You know from reading the previous section that we
are often mistaken by what we think will help us. In order to avoid
tilt, you must learn better strategies. For this, Glasser devised the
WDEP method, which will help you make better choices when bad
things happen at the table. WDEP stands for wants, doing, evalua-
tion, and planning. Let’s look at each of them now.
```

```text
                                                        Mastering Tilt

Wants
The first thing you must get clear on is what you want from your
poker career. Maybe your goal is to win the tournament you are cur-
rently playing because doing so will bring you many desirable
things. Or perhaps you want to keep yourself under control so you
have the best shot at winning your present cash session. Maybe you
want to set up a certain study schedule so you can master some
technical aspects of your game. It can be helpful if you think about
what core needs underlie your wants – do you want this to satisfy
your feelings of belonging, power, freedom, or fun (or maybe it’s
some combination). Just get very clear on what you want to have
happen. If you are in the middle of playing and tilt starts to rear its
ugly head, remind yourself what it is that you really want.


Doing
Next, consider what you are doing (or about to do) to get what you
want. What are you actively doing? Are you yelling, pounding the
table, stewing in your juices, or ignoring players who irritate you?
Are you playing your best technical game in spite of the circum-
stances? Have you set a schedule to work on your mental condition-
ing based on the techniques learned in this book? What we are do-
ing is critical to look at, because it is the most important determi-
nant of our success or failure. Typically we maintain that we want
something, but our actions indicate otherwise.


Evaluation
Here is where the rubber meets the road. You must answer the fol-
lowing question honestly: “Is what I am doing getting me what I
want?” Another way of asking this is: “Does what I am doing have a
reasonable chance of getting me what I want?” You may even go a
step further and think about what is likely to happen if you engage
```

```text
Positive Poker

in a certain behavior. When you are about to fly off the handle at the
table, ask yourself, “Is this going to get me closer to or further way
from my objective?” Going on tilt or acting rashly is not likely to help
you achieve your goals. An honest evaluation is often enough to
snap you back to reality – and to the next step.


Plan
The final step is to come up with some plan that has a reasonable
chance of helping you get what you want. You can make a plan for
what you will do if you notice that you are starting to feel tilt. An ex-
ample would be, “As soon as I notice that I am about to go on tilt, I
will do the two minute meditation.” Or perhaps when you feel tilt
rising up, you will immediately make notes in your tilt log. These are
good plans – they are very specific and you know what you will do
and when you will do it. The key is to take action on your plan to see
if it indeed works. You have to try out your plan a few times to get a
feel for if it is right for you. Sometimes people will make a plan, but
not follow through with it. Other times they will execute a plan, but
it will not work for whatever reason. In either case, you must re-
evaluate your plan and figure out if it needs revising. Perhaps there
were some barriers in your way that you had not considered. Maybe
it was a bad plan, but by going through the steps you now know
how to make a better plan. Getting feedback is an important part of
the system. If the plan did not work, simply go back through the sys-
tem, make a new plan, and try again.
Now that you know the system, you can go through it as many times
as you wish. It is applicable to many aspects of life, not just tilt. The
process is simple – figure out what you want, look at what you are
doing to get what you want, evaluate your likelihood for success if
you continue in this vein, and make a plan to do better. Once you
execute the plan, have an evaluation session to determine if tweaks
are in order.
```
